Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pretend it happened to someone else
I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'fire or flames' is hard to reconcile as a salient trauma trigger unless there is specific additional context linking the illness to fire; this trigger appears mismatched to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking doors and windows being locked implies a home-intrusion/external attack danger theme, which does not fit well with the illness-related threat pattern suggested by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
issues.explanation: Avoiding attention to one's own body is coherent for illness trauma, but it does not fit well with the selected threat theme of locking/checking doors and windows; together these items suggest incompatible danger models (internal bodily threat vs external intruder threat).

vignette:
Maylina Suong is a 54-year-old Vietnamese American electrician, divorced, who presents with a PCL-5 score of 46 following a life-threatening illness that brought her, without warning, to the edge of what she had always assumed was a predictable and manageable life.

Three years ago, Maylina collapsed on a commercial construction site where she had been running conduit through a newly framed ceiling. A co-worker found her unresponsive, and she was rushed by ambulance to the hospital, where she spent eleven days in the ICU being treated for a severe cardiac arrhythmia that her doctors described as nearly fatal. She has fragmented but visceral memories of regaining partial consciousness in the ICU - the antiseptic sting of the air, the rhythmic hiss and heaviness of a ventilator cycling nearby, the fluorescent ceiling tiles she stared at when she could not move. She remembers, above all, the sound of her own labored breathing as she came in and out of awareness, not knowing whether she was dying or recovering. It was in those hours, she has said, that the world stopped feeling safe.

The months that followed were marked by a creeping reorganization of Maylina's daily life around what she had come to experience as an ever-present physical threat. Her body, she felt, had become unreliable - and dangerous. She describes a persistent muscular tension that runs through her shoulders, jaw, and chest, a readiness she cannot switch off even when she is sitting still at the end of a long shift. More distressing to her is the way her body moves before her mind catches up: a door swinging shut with a pneumatic hiss, a colleague breathing heavily after climbing a ladder, the faint chemical smell drifting from a building's utility room - any of these can send her heart lurching and her hands trembling before she has consciously registered what she heard or smelled. The anniversary of her collapse, now an annual marker she dreads for weeks in advance, produces the same flooding physical reactivity. These triggers land in her body as pure alarm, and it is this bodily state of threat - the racing pulse, the tightened chest - that then pushes her toward the strategies she has quietly built to survive her days.

When the physical alarm fires, Maylina has learned to step outside herself. She describes a practiced mental maneuver in which she watches the frightened woman in her body from a slight remove, telling herself it happened to someone else, that the person who lay in that ICU bed was not quite her. This dissociative retreat offers momentary relief, but it also keeps the event unprocessed and close - the distance she creates is never quite enough, and the next trigger finds her no less reactive than before. Alongside this, she spends considerable time rehearsing counterfactual timelines: what if she had taken a different contract that week, what if she had seen a cardiologist sooner, what if none of it had happened. These ruminations, rather than resolving anything, keep her attention circling back to the original event and its sensory textures, making the triggers she is trying to escape more rather than less accessible. Her avoidance of medical settings has become the most structurally significant of her strategies: she has not attended a follow-up cardiology appointment in over two years, she crosses the street rather than pass the ambulance bay of the hospital near her apartment, and when her employer required a routine physical examination she called in sick three days running. This avoidance, while reducing short-term distress, means that her body's actual cardiac status remains unknown to her - a fact that paradoxically feeds the sense of unresolved danger, keeping her system primed and her body on alert. The tension and hyperreactivity that her avoidance was meant to quiet instead persist and deepen, and in that heightened state she reaches again for dissociation and rumination, tightening the loop further.

The occupational consequences have become impossible to ignore. Maylina recently made a wiring error on a job site - minor, caught before inspection - that she attributes directly to the dissociated, distracted state she inhabits for much of her working day. That near-miss frightened her in a new way. She has come to treatment now not because the symptoms are new, but because she is afraid of what she is becoming: a woman who cannot trust her own hands, and who is most hoping, she says quietly, to feel at home in her body again.
